title: The heart's polish
hook: a well-known saying: everything has a polish, and the heart's polish is remembrance (Bayhaqi)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ikhtilaf: some love the Sufi orders and shrines, others see them as later additions, and all say keep to the Qur'an. Your line: the same Qur'an underneath.

Before glass mirrors, a mirror was a disc of metal: bronze, silver, polished steel. Leave one in a damp room for a season and it clouds over. Your face in it goes dim, then disappears. Nobody throws the mirror away. You take a cloth, you rub, and your face comes back. A well-known saying, recorded by the scholar al-Bayhaqi and attributed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: everything has something that polishes it, and the polish of the heart is the remembrance of Allah. Scholars discuss how strong its chain of narrators is, but the picture has lasted. It closes the Sufi path.
screen: `A METAL MIRROR, CLOUDED OVER.` → `A CLOTH, AND YOUR FACE COMES BACK.` → `THE POLISH OF THE HEART.`

segments.voice: The picture starts in the Qur'an. Speaking of people who have hardened themselves against the truth, it says, in Pickthall's words: "Nay, but that which they have earned is rust upon their hearts." The Arabic word is ran: a film, a tarnish. A hadith in Tirmidhi explains it. When a person does wrong, a dark spot appears on the heart. If they stop, turn back and ask forgiveness, the heart is polished clean. If they keep going, the spot spreads, and that is the ran Allah mentions. So the heart isn't bad. It's a mirror that picks up dust, and the cloth is dhikr, the same work the circles do aloud or in silence. Al-Ghazali, after his crisis, wrote of the heart as a mirror that can show the truth once it's cleaned. Rumi tells a story in the Masnavi: the Chinese and the Greeks hold a painting contest. The Chinese cover their wall with color. The Greeks paint nothing. They polish their wall, and when the curtain between the two is lifted, it shines back everything the Chinese painted, and more. Rumi says the Greeks are like the Sufis, who have polished their hearts. Rabi'a's love, Junayd's sobriety, the reed flute's longing, the circles of gathered remembrance, the nafs being trained: under each is the same slow work with the cloth. And remember yesterday: not every Muslim walks the Sufi orders, but the call to remember Allah comes from the Qur'an itself, and belongs to no single group.
screen: `RUST UPON THEIR HEARTS` · `A MIRROR THAT PICKS UP DUST` · `THE CLOTH IS REMEMBRANCE` · `THE GREEKS POLISHED THEIR WALL`

segments.voice: A pattern from a hadith in al-Bukhari, which the Prophet taught his daughter Fatimah for bedtime: SubhanAllah thirty-three times, alhamdulillah thirty-three, Allahu akbar thirty-four. If you pray, say them softly now, counting on your fingers; if you're learning, say one phrase at a time, each one a single pass of the cloth. Slowly matters more than finishing, and you can finish the hundred afterward.
Dhikr. Remembrance of God — the cloth that, a hadith says, polishes the dust a heart gathers. Today's word.
Your line: polish the heart. Day three hundred eight, and the Sufi path is complete.

howItsDone: Many Muslims say SubhanAllah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar thirty-three or thirty-four times each after prayer or before sleep, often counting on the fingers or on prayer beads, and speak of remembrance as what keeps the heart clear.
